name: Golden toad
intro: Zib! Monteverde, Costa Rica, 1987. It's so misty up here Glorp can barely see, but somewhere in these puddles are toads that glow bright orange.
description: The golden toad lived only in a tiny patch, about 4 km², of misty cloud forest on a mountain ridge above Monteverde, Costa Rica. Males were a shining orange-gold; females were dark olive with red-edged spots. For most of the year they hid underground, then came out for a few weeks in the spring rains to breed in small pools. In 1987 scientists counted about 1,500 adults. The next year only a handful appeared, and in 1989 a single male was seen. It was never found again. Its loss is linked to an unusually warm, dry El Niño year and to chytrid, a fungus that has killed frogs and toads around the world, though scientists still debate exactly what happened.

facts.cause: Probably a very dry, warm year plus chytrid fungus disease (still debated)

habitat.biome: Tropical cloud forest (elfin forest) on a mountain ridge
habitat.climate: Cool, misty and wet almost all year

terrain.value: Mossy cloud forest floor with shallow rain pools
terrain.why: It hid underground in the forest and bred in small, shallow pools left by the rain.

temperature.why: High up on the mountain the tropics are cool, and it never had to cope with real heat.

humidity.why: Toads breathe partly through their skin, which must stay wet, and this forest lives inside the clouds.

oxygen.why: Ordinary air, which it partly breathed through its skin.

pressure.why: It lived about 1,500 m up a mountain, where the air pressure is lower than at sea level.

hotspots.label: Rain pool
hotspots.fact: A shallow pool left by the rain. Golden toads gathered in pools like this for a few weeks each spring to breed.

hotspots.label: Drifting mist
hotspots.fact: This forest sits inside the clouds. A toad's skin must stay wet, because it breathes partly through it.

hotspots.label: Dripping moss
hotspots.fact: Everything is covered in moss. High on the mountain it's cool, even though this is the tropics.

hotspots.label: Mountain ridge
hotspots.fact: We're about 1,500 m up, where the air pressure is lower than at sea level.

hotspots.label: Golden male
hotspots.fact: A male golden toad, bright orange like a jelly sweet! Only the males were this colour.

hotspots.label: Spotted female
hotspots.fact: Females looked completely different: dark olive with red-edged spots. In 1987 scientists counted about 1,500 toads here.

hotspots.label: Strings of eggs
hotspots.fact: Toad eggs, laid in strings in the pool. By 1989 only one male would turn up, and then none ever again.
